newsitem.title: USA: AT&T sees competition hurting second half profits.
newsitem.headline: AT&T sees competition hurting second half profits.

text.p: AT&T Corp., citing competition in its key long-distance telephone business, warned Tuesday that its quarterly earnings would not meet Wall Street's expectations.
The telecommunications giant also launched a new long-distance programme, joining the ranks of competitors Sprint Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. with less-complicated price structures.
AT&T said its third-quarter earnings could be as much as 10 percent below Wall Street estimates and that the pressure would continue for the rest of the year.
The news sparked a sell-off in the company's stock, which is the most widely held in North America.
AT&T fell $5.75 to $51.50 after a delayed opening on the New York Stock Exchange, and more than 15 million shares had changed hands by the closing bell.

Chairman Robert Allen said in a statement that AT&T's third-quarter results appeared to be as much as 10 percent below analysts' mean estimate of 92 cents a share and that the fourth quarter will likely fall short of the mean estimate of 89 cents a share.
In the second quarter, AT&T earned $1.49 billion, or 92 cents a share, on revenues of $13 billion.
Allen also said the company's earnings were being affected by its investments in local, on-line and wireless services as well as infrastucture to provide new communications and information services.
"Further, we currently believe that competitive pressures will continue for the remainder of the year, and we are intensifying our marketing efforts," Allen said.
He said the company had been hurt by competition from other long-distance telephone companies.
"While we have succeeded in stabilising volumes and revenues at last quarter's levels, the number of customers moving between carriers is still disturbing," he said.
"Our research indicates that this customer volatility is due largely to price misperceptions that are frequently promoted by some competitors."
In a conference call with analysts and reporters, Richard Miller, AT&T chief financial officer, said the company was "taking more aggressive action on sales and marketing."
Allen added, "We're greatly accelerating our expenditures."
The announcement of a drop in earnings comes as AT&T finishes splitting itself up in a massive restructuring.
AT&T will complete the spin-off of its Lucent Technologies Inc. telecommunications equipment subsidiary on Sept. 30. AT&T is also spinning off its NCR Corp. computer unit.
As part of the restructuring, AT&T also is making a major reduction in its workforce. Allen said that reduction was "on track" and would lead to about 17,000 job cuts.
Industry analysts at several Wall Street brokerages lowered their ratings on AT&T as a result of the news.

"Mother Bell has been a sacred cow until now. This type of news is going to be disquieting," said Fahnestock & Co. market analyst Alan Ackerman. "It's likely to put a lot of pressure on the stock and ruffle the feathers of many shareholders."

In a separate announcement Tuesday, the company took aim at competitors with a new long-distance calling plan that would give consumers the option of a flat calling rate of 15 cents a minute at any time to anywhere in the United States.
In response to AT&T's statement, Sprint, a key competitor in the long-distance market, said it was gaining market share and had not suffered any similar setback to its results.

Sprint, which advertises its long distance rate as 10 cents a minute, said its long-distance consumer business grew at a rate three times faster than AT&T's consumer business during the first half of this year.
"Thus far through the third quarter of 1996, Sprint is seeing the simplicity of it's dime-a-minute message continue to drive record sales," the company said.
